setup.zh: 八月，马家花三百两给马小宝买了一张荐书，名册上还要马三画押。那一缕热卡在心口底下，沉不下去。九月初四夜里，爹从墙上摘下了那张弓；娘给了你针线和一个空钱袋。
setup.en: In the eighth month the Mas spend three hundred taels on a letter of recommendation for Ma Xiaobao, and the village roll still needs Ma San's signature. The thread of warmth is stuck under your heart and won't sink. On the night of the fourth of the ninth month Father takes the bow down from the wall; Mother gives you needle and thread and an empty purse.

recap.zh: 爹把爷爷的弓给了你，娘给了你针线和一个空钱袋：「你自己挣满它。」
recap.en: Father gave you grandfather's bow, and Mother needle and thread and an empty purse: "Fill it yourself."

zh: 娘的针线，和一个空钱袋。
en: Father takes the old bow down from the wall.
Mother's needle and thread, and an empty purse.

story.zh:
八月里，沉鼎观开山门的消息，传遍了四乡。马家老爷备了整整三百两银子的礼，打发马三连夜上山，给马小宝讨来一封「荐书」。三百两，是沈家一百多年的租。马三在村口的酒桌上喝得满脸通红：「有荐书，灵根差一点也收！我那表哥，在观里管名册二十几年，谁家孩子什么根骨，他一看一个准——太华山上的仙长，都找他！我家小宝，将来是要做仙师的！」马三一拍桌子，又道：「到时候，蒙山上的风——」村里人齐声接口，十分熟练：「姓马！」

荐书是马小宝一个人的，名册却是全村的。告示上写着「身家清白者」，县里派了一个老差役下乡收名册，一村一张，要村里的大户画押作保。石坳村的大户，只有马家。

差役是个瘦老头，一天要跑五个村，只想赶在天黑前吃上一口热饭。他在马家门口摊开名册，马三捏着笔，念一个名字，画一个押，念到「沈小满」，笔停了：「沈家欠着马家的租，不清白。这个押，不画。」差役看看马三，又看看日头：「欠多少？」马三张嘴就道：「前年那张皮，去年的肉——」

「三爷。」小满他娘不知什么时候站在了人群前头，手里捧着那叠账纸，「前年的欠，是那张鹿皮；去年的租，二十斤肉，三爷家的家丁亲手称的；今年的租，秋收才到日子。去年冬月廿二，山风钱一百五十文，三爷亲手收的。」她一页一页地翻，一行一行地念，念得跟念经一样平。

差役接过账纸看了看，翻到末一页，指着那十个字：「这一页画了三个圈，是什么账？」四下里一静。小满站在人群后头，一颗心提到了嗓子眼。他娘面不改色：「鸡。抱窝的那只，蹲了一冬，孵出来三个，还有七个没出壳。」差役「哦」了一声，把账纸还给她，对马三道：「账是清的。画押。」他还要赶下一个村。

马三捏着笔，看了小满他娘很久，终于还是画了。画完了，他把笔往桌上一搁：「画了，也得爬得上去。三百级石阶，你家那小子，挑两桶水都喘。」

那天夜里，小满坐在柴垛上，咬着牙。「挑两桶水都喘」，这句话在他心口里打转，转一圈，那口气便往上一顶。他想起正月那一夜，柴垛顶上，他爹压着嗓子说的那一句：它听见的不是你喘，是你心慌。他便松了牙，不去压它，也不去数，只把那口气细细地吐，吐完了，再细细地吸，像他娘拨算盘，一颗是一颗。不知坐到了几更，心口底下那只卡了一夏天的水桶，忽然「咯噔」一声，自己往下走了：那一缕热沉过心口，沉到肚脐，稳稳地落住了。再往下，便没了。他不知道底下是什么，只知道这一回，热沉下去了，再没浮上来。

第二天一早，他娘在账本最末一页的「下」字外头，画了第四个圈。画完了，把账本摊在炕桌上晾墨，自去灶前烧火。他爹拖着腿过来，低头看了半天。那十个字，他只认得这一个：山下、坡下、树底下，下套子的下。他拿粗指头在那个新圈旁边按了按，没敢碰着墨，问：「往下沉了？」小满道：「嗯。」他爹道：「那就稳了。」

那几日，刘豆芽去马家放羊了。老刘家开春借了马家两斗米，利滚利，到八月还不上，大小子便去马家放羊抵债。他赶着羊从沈家门口过，没抬头。

傍晚，阿禾在井台边上拦住他：「泗水几天的路？」「三天。」「一天吃几张饼？」「一张。」阿禾从耳朵上取下炭条，在一个蓝布面的小本子上记了一笔，转身走了。那本子，小满从没见过。

九月初四夜里，他爹坐在炕沿上，一只手按着膝盖，指头一下一下地敲着炕桌，敲了很久。然后他站起来，一瘸一拐地走到墙边，把那张缠着牛筋的旧弓摘了下来，放在儿子面前：「你爷爷的。你拿着。」小满道：「……爹，这话听着像骂人。」「不许瞎说。」他爹把弓往他怀里一塞，「你爷爷的弓。」

弓背上十七道牛筋，缠得紧紧的，是爷爷缠的，他爹重缠过的。他爹道：「到了沉鼎山，石阶是一炷香三百级。你舅舅爬到一百七十级——他说的。」他教小满：三步一吸，三步一呼，吸的时候气往下沉，呼的时候脚往前送；不看坡顶，只看脚底下这一级。「追兔子比快，追鹿比稳。山上的路，都是这么走完的。」他顿了一顿，又道：「往后一个人拉弓，没人在你身后说先看风了，你得自己说。」

他爹又道：「到了仙家门派，要守人家的规矩。要老实。别跟人争——」他娘道：「他爹。」他爹便不说了。

他娘从怀里摸出一个小布包，是一套针线：一个顶针，三根针，一卷黑线，一卷白线。还有一个钱袋，青布缝的，针脚细细密密，袋口穿着一根红绳。钱袋是空的。「针线，衣裳破了自己补。」别人家的娘，临行密密缝；他娘把针给了他。她拿指头点了点那个钱袋，「钱袋是空的。你自己，挣满它。」

她看着他，又道：「你爹的话，你听一半。要守规矩——对。要老实——对好人老实。别跟人争——」说到这里，她停住了，伸手把他的衣领翻好，抻平了，才道：

「争得过，再争。」

油灯的火苗跳了一跳。她那只翻衣领的手，翻完了，在他的肩膀上停了一停。
story.en:
In the eighth month word that Chending Temple was opening its gate went round all the villages. Master Ma got together a gift of three hundred taels and sent Ma San up the mountain overnight to beg a letter of recommendation for Ma Xiaobao. Three hundred taels was more than a hundred years of the Shens' rent. At the wine table by the village gate Ma San drank himself red in the face: "With a recommendation, they take you even if your roots are a bit short! My cousin's kept the temple roll twenty-odd years — what bones a child's got, he can tell at a glance — even the immortals on Mount Taihua come to him! My Xiaobao's going to be an immortal master!" Ma San slapped the table. "And then the wind on Mount Meng —" The villagers chimed in together, well practised: "— is named Ma!"

The letter of recommendation was Ma Xiaobao's alone, but the roll was the whole village's. The notice said *of clean family*; the county sent an old runner round the villages to collect the rolls, one sheet a village, each to be signed as guarantee by the village's big household. Shi'ao Village's big household was the Mas, and only the Mas.

The runner was a skinny old man with five villages to do in a day and only one wish — a hot meal before dark. He spread the roll at the Mas' gate; Ma San held the brush, read out a name, signed; at *Shen Xiaoman* the brush stopped. "The Shens owe the Mas rent. Not clean. I won't sign this one." The runner looked at Ma San, then at the sun. "Owe how much?" Ma San opened his mouth at once: "The hide from the year before last, last year's meat —"

"Third Master." At some point Xiaoman's mother had come to stand at the front of the crowd, holding that stack of account sheets. "The arrears from the year before last — that was the deer hide. Last year's rent — twenty catties of meat, weighed by your own men. this year's rent isn't due till the harvest. Last year, the twenty-second of the eleventh month, mountain-wind money, a hundred and fifty cash, taken by your own hand, Third Master." She turned page after page and read line after line, flat as reciting a sutra.

The runner took the sheets and looked through them, turned to the last page and pointed at the ten characters. "This page — three circles. What account is this?" Everything went quiet. Xiaoman, at the back of the crowd, had his heart in his throat. His mother didn't blink. "A hen. The broody one. Sat all winter, hatched three, seven still in the shell." The runner said "Ah," handed the sheets back, and told Ma San, "The accounts are clean. Sign." He still had another village to do.

Ma San held the brush and looked at Xiaoman's mother a long time, and in the end he signed. When he'd done he put the brush down on the table. "Signed — he still has to climb it. Three hundred stone steps, and that boy of yours pants carrying two buckets of water."

That night Xiaoman sat on the woodpile with his teeth clenched. *Pants carrying two buckets of water* — the words went round and round in his chest, and each time round the breath shoved upward. He remembered that night in the first month, on top of the woodpile, the words his father said under his breath: *It's not your breathing it hears. It's your fear.* So he unclenched his teeth, didn't push it, didn't count, only breathed out fine and slow, and when it was out breathed in fine and slow, like his mother flicking the abacus, one bead at a time. Some watch of the night — he never knew which — the bucket stuck under his heart all summer suddenly went *clunk* and moved down of itself: the thread of warmth sank past the heart, down to the navel, and came to rest, steady. Further down there was nothing. He didn't know what lay below; he only knew that this time the warmth had sunk, and didn't float back up.

Early next morning his mother drew a fourth circle, round the character *down* on the last page of her ledger. Then she left the ledger open on the kang table for the ink to dry and went to light the stove. His father dragged his leg over and looked at it a long time. Of those ten characters he knew only this one: downhill, down the slope, down under a tree, set a snare down. He pressed a thick finger beside the new circle, careful not to touch the ink. "Gone down, has it?" Xiaoman said, "Mm." His father said, "Then you're steady."

Those days Liu Douya went to herd the Mas' sheep. In spring the Lius had borrowed two pecks of rice from the Mas; with the interest rolling, by the eighth month they couldn't pay, so the eldest boy went to herd sheep against the debt. He drove the sheep past the Shens' door and didn't look up.

At dusk Ahe stopped him by the well. "How many days to the Si River?" "Three." "How many flatbreads a day?" "One." Ahe took the stick of charcoal from behind her ear, made a note in a small blue-covered book, and walked off. Xiaoman had never seen that book before.

On the night of the fourth of the ninth month his father sat on the edge of the kang, one hand on his knee, tapping the kang table with a finger, a long time. Then he stood, limped to the wall, took down the old sinew-wrapped bow and set it before his son. "Your grandpa's. You take it." Xiaoman said, "…Dad, that sounds like swearing." "Don't talk nonsense." His father pushed the bow into his arms. "Your grandpa's bow."

Seventeen turns of ox sinew on the back of the bow, wound tight — wound by his grandfather, rewound by his father. His father said, "At Chending Mountain the steps are three hundred in one stick of incense. Your uncle got to the hundred and seventieth — so he says." He taught Xiaoman: three steps breathing in, three steps breathing out; breathing in, let the breath sink; breathing out, push the foot forward; don't look at the top of the slope, only at the step under your feet. "Chasing a hare, you need speed. Chasing a deer, you need steadiness. Every road up a mountain gets walked like that." He paused, and added: "From now on you draw a bow alone; there's nobody behind you saying 'read the wind first'. You have to say it yourself."

His father went on, "In an immortals' sect, you keep their rules. Be honest. Don't fight with people —" His mother said, "His dad." His father stopped.

His mother took a little cloth bundle from her coat: a sewing kit — a thimble, three needles, a reel of black thread, a reel of white. And a purse, sewn of blue cloth, the stitches fine and close, a red cord through the mouth. The purse was empty. "Needle and thread — when your clothes tear, mend them yourself." Other boys' mothers stitch close and tight before the son sets out; his mother gave him the needle. She tapped the purse with a finger. "The purse is empty. You fill it yourself."

She looked at him and said: "Of your father's words, listen to half. Keep the rules — right. Be honest — honest with good people. Don't fight with people —" here she stopped, reached out and turned his collar straight, smoothed it flat, and only then said:

"If you can win, then fight."

The lamp flame jumped. The hand that had turned his collar, once done, rested on his shoulder a moment.

label.en: The sixth of the ninth month: set off for the Si River

exits.means: sets off for the trials at the temple

story.zh:
走的前一夜，小满去了一趟村北，在锁儿的坟前站了一会儿，把那块木板上叫雨泡模糊了的字，又一笔一笔刻深了。从坟上下来，他去了一趟村东头。吴婆婆照旧坐在门槛上，拿一把破蒲扇一下一下地扇脚底下。他还没开口，她已道：「要走了。」小满在门槛边上坐下，等着她说那九句废话，好把那一句能救命的捞出来带走。吴婆婆却道：「婆婆今儿不说废话了。只说一句。饿了，就吃。饱了，就放下。」小满等了一会儿：「……就这一句？」「就这一句。回罢。你娘在烙饼。」走出去几步，吴婆婆在身后又道：「那块牌子，贴肉揣着。别叫它冷着。」他回头，她咧开嘴，露出那三颗牙来：「婆婆这三颗牙，在等一样东西。等到了，才肯掉。」说完便扇起了蒲扇，脸朝着西边，不再理他了。

那是他在柴垛上的最后一夜。他坐了一个时辰，数了一回：九十六。鹅毛在他鼻子底下抖着，抖得很轻，像风过了以后，草尖上还剩下的那一点。没停。

九月初五。满，九十六。毛抖。

他娘把这一行写完，搁下了笔。一百二十，还差二十四。

临走前，他娘塞给他一个布包，里头是四张饼，是前一夜烙的。小满半夜醒来，看见灶间的油灯亮着——那灯芯头一回没掐短，火苗有指头那么大——他娘站在灶前，一张一张地烙。「路上吃。一天一张，吃到泗水。」小满数了数：「娘，到泗水三天，多了一张。」他娘道：「打不过，就跑。跑饿了，吃那一张。」她又塞给他一个小本子，是拿舅舅带来的那包红糖的包纸订的，封皮上还透着一点甜味。「一个人进山门，身上没个账本可不行。空的，你自己记。」一个空钱袋，一个空本子。小满把那根鹅毛夹进了本子的第一页。

走的那天，是九月初六，天还没亮。舅舅在济世堂告了几天假，头天夜里便到了，要一路送他走到泗水；他爹送他们到县城。他娘没有送，她说家里得有人看着灶。她站在老槐树底下，两只手拢在袖子里，一动不动，像去年秋天那样。小满背着弓，揣着针线、空钱袋、空本子、四张饼，还有怀里那锭圈里一横的银子，走过老槐树的时候，回头看了一眼。他娘的一只手从袖子里抬了起来，停在半空里，没有挥，也没有放下来。那一天碗碎的时候，他娘伸出去捞碗，也是这样停在半空里的。

他本以为阿禾会在那里，跟他算一算账，说一句「三个半，别忘了」。她不在。他又回头看了一眼，还是不在。羊坡上，刘豆芽赶着马家的羊，远远地朝他举了举鞭子。

他转过身，跟着他爹和舅舅往村外走去。离九月初九，还有三天；离一百二十，还差二十四。走出村口半里地，日头出来了，他忽然觉出胸口那块木牌是温的。白天，它向来是凉的；他两只手一直拢在袖子里，一回也没碰过它。他站住了，隔着衣裳按住它，心里头一回冒出一句话来：

……那是谁捂的？
story.en:
The night before he left, Xiaoman went north of the village and stood a while at Suo'er's grave, and recut, stroke by stroke, the character the rain had worn soft on the board. Coming down from the grave he went to the east end. Granny Wu sat on her threshold as always, fanning her feet with a broken rush fan. Before he spoke she said, "You're leaving." Xiaoman sat down by the threshold to wait for her nine sentences of nonsense, so he could fish out the one that saves a life and take it with him. But Granny Wu said: "Granny isn't talking nonsense today. Just one thing. When you're hungry, eat. When you're full, put it down." Xiaoman waited. "…That's it?" "That's it. Go home. Your mother's making flatbread." He'd gone a few steps when Granny Wu spoke behind him again: "That token — keep it against your skin. Don't let it get cold." He turned; she grinned, showing her three teeth. "Granny's three teeth are waiting for something. Only when it comes will they fall." Then she was fanning again, face to the west, and paid him no more mind.

It was his last night on the woodpile. He sat for an hour and counted once: ninety-six. The goose feather trembled under his nose, trembled very lightly, like what's left on the grass tips after the wind has passed. It didn't stop.

Ninth month, fifth. Man: ninety-six. Feather trembled.

His mother finished writing that line and put down the brush. A hundred and twenty, still twenty-four short.

Before he left, his mother pressed a cloth bundle on him: four flatbreads, made the night before. Xiaoman had woken in the night and seen the oil lamp lit in the kitchen — the first time its wick hadn't been pinched short, the flame as big as a finger — and his mother standing at the stove making them one by one. "For the road. One a day, all the way to the Si River." Xiaoman counted. "Ma, it's three days to the Si River. That's one too many." His mother said, "If you can't win, run. When running makes you hungry, eat that one." She also gave him a little notebook, bound from the paper that had wrapped the brown sugar Uncle brought, the cover still faintly sweet. "Going into a mountain gate on your own, you can't be without an account book. It's blank; keep it yourself." An empty purse, an empty book. Xiaoman tucked the goose feather into the book's first page.

The day he left was the sixth of the ninth month, before light. Uncle had taken a few days' leave from the Jishi Hall and arrived the night before, to see him all the way to the Si River; his father would see them as far as the county town. His mother didn't come; someone, she said, had to mind the stove. She stood under the old locust tree, hands tucked in her sleeves, not moving, as she had last autumn. Xiaoman, with the bow on his back and in his jacket the needle and thread, the empty purse, the empty book, the four flatbreads, and the silver ingot with the circle and the stroke, looked back once as he passed the old locust tree. One of his mother's hands rose out of her sleeve and stopped in mid-air; it didn't wave, and didn't come down. The day the bowl broke, when his mother reached for it, her hand had stopped in mid-air just like that.

He'd thought A He would be there, to settle accounts with him and say "three and a half, don't forget". She wasn't. He looked back again; still not there. On the sheep slope Liu Douya, driving the Mas' sheep, raised his whip to him from far off.

He turned and followed his father and his uncle out of the village. Three days to the ninth of the ninth; twenty-four short of a hundred and twenty. Half a li past the village gate the sun came up, and he suddenly felt that the token on his chest was warm. By day it was always cool; both hands had been tucked in his sleeves all along, and he hadn't touched it once. He stopped, pressed it through his clothes, and for the first time a thought came to him:

…Then who warmed it?
